segments.title: Opening: The Fog and Its Secrets

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a series dedicated to one of the most ambitious, maddening, and magnificent novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be moving through Bleak House chapter by chapter — its fog, its satire, its grief, and its extraordinary human warmth.
Three brilliant minds are joining me for the journey, and I want to introduce them properly, because each brings something the novel genuinely needs.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads prose the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — she sees exactly how it's been assembled, and why.
For a novel as architecturally complex as Bleak House, that eye for craft is indispensable.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian, and Bleak House is, among other things, a sustained assault on the English legal system.
James will tell us what the institutions actually were, what they cost ordinary people, and why Dickens's anger was entirely justified.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novel audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to Bleak House as a performer who hears the prose from the inside.
If anyone can tell us what this novel sounds like at full volume, it's Oliver.
Today's opening segment takes us into some of the novel's most distinctive territory — family, secrecy, and the strange human shapes that circumstance creates.
James, I want to start with you, because you've been looking at the Smallweed family, and there is something almost anthropological in the way Dickens describes them.
The Smallweeds are one of Dickens's most controlled comic inventions — but the comedy is inseparable from a genuine sociological argument.
What he's describing, with deadpan precision, is the effect of a single-minded commercial culture transmitted across three generations.
The grandfather goes out early into commerce, marries late, produces a lean and anxious son, who does exactly the same, who produces Bartholomew and Judith Smallweed — twins.
Each generation, the narrator tells us, has discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, and fables — and banished all levities whatsoever.
The cumulative result of this relentless pruning is what Dickens delivers as a kind of triumphant conclusion — and the word 'gratifying' does a great deal of ironic work.

"Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds."
Old monkeys with something depressing on their minds — that is a sentence written for posterity.
And the historical point underneath the joke is serious: this is what the moneylending and discounting trades actually did to family life in nineteenth-century London.
What strikes me about that passage is the architecture of accumulation — the narrator mimics the very process being described.
Each clause repeats the generational pattern — going out early, marrying late — and the prose itself becomes a kind of treadmill.
And then Dickens releases the tension with that single devastating image, delivered with mock solemnity as though it were a public health statistic.
The word 'observed' is doing wonderful work — as if naturalists had been out in the field, taking notes on the Smallweed specimens.
The comedy lives entirely in the delivery — and the key, as Eleanor says, is that mock-clinical register.
When I've read this passage aloud, the temptation is to play it for laughs, but the funnier choice is to play it straight — to commit fully to the solemnity.
'Something depressing on their minds' — that little trailing qualifier is where the genius is.
It's not just depressed monkeys — it's monkeys with something specific and unspecified weighing on them, and Dickens trusts you to feel the comedy of that precision.
Skimpole, of course, is the other side of that coin — and the passage Esther gives us of his lodgings is equally precise, in a quite different register.
Where the Smallweeds have stripped every pleasure from life in the name of commerce, Skimpole has abolished every responsibility in the name of pleasure.
Esther describes his sitting room, and the detail Dickens chooses tells you everything.

"It was dingy enough and not at all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music, newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures."
Broken pane of glass papered over — but a plate of hothouse nectarines on the table, and a bottle of light wine.
That juxtaposition of squalor and luxury is not accidental — it is a portrait of a man who has entirely externalised the costs of his pleasures onto everyone around him.
And 'shabby luxury' is a perfect two-word novel in itself — you know exactly the sort of person who inhabits it before you've met him.
There he is, reclined on his sofa in a dressing-gown at midday, drinking fragrant coffee from an old china cup, studying wallflowers.
Dickens gives you the old china cup — not just a cup, an old china cup — because Skimpole insists on the aesthetic dimension of his own degradation.
He is a comic villain of the most insidious kind — one who has turned irresponsibility into an art form.
What's remarkable is how Dickens manages to make Skimpole charming — genuinely charming — even as he's showing you the mechanism of the charm.
That's a very difficult novelistic trick — to make the reader feel what the character's victims feel, while simultaneously seeing through it.
Esther, as narrator, is both seduced and unsettled, and we feel both at once, because her narration is doing the same double work.
Which brings us to Esther herself — and a passage that moves the novel into entirely different emotional territory.
Oliver, you've been looking at the scene where Esther and her mother finally meet — and I know that's a passage you feel strongly about.
Strongly is an understatement — it's one of the great scenes of restraint in Victorian fiction, and it almost shouldn't work.
Esther's narration throughout has been careful, modest — she qualifies everything she says about herself.
But here, in this scene, the emotion breaks through the careful prose, and Dickens lets it come in fragments.
Listen to how she describes what she tried to say to her mother — the very syntax enacts the difficulty of it.
"I told her — or I tried to tell her — that if it were for me, her child, under any circumstances to take upon me to forgive her, I did it, and had done it, many, many years."
That dash — 'or I tried to tell her' — is the whole emotional truth of the moment, compressed into five words.
She didn't fully manage it. Language failed her. Dickens admits that, and it makes the scene more devastating, not less.
And what she does manage to say, when language holds long enough — that's where the most extraordinary line in the passage lands.
She reaches for something that sounds almost like a formal declaration — her sense of duty — and then it opens into something much larger.
"My duty was to bless her and receive her, though the whole world turned from her, and that I only asked her leave to do it."
'I only asked her leave to do it' — that clause, at the end, is the emotional core of Esther's entire character.
She is asserting profound love while still deferring — she is asking permission to love her own mother.
No other character in this novel is drawn with quite that psychological subtlety, and it sits in a sentence you might almost miss on a fast reading.
The burden Esther carries isn't only emotional — it's existential in a very concrete sense.
The passage we're also looking at from Esther's narration in Chapter 43 makes the danger terrifyingly specific.
Her mother has told her to consider her dead — and Esther cannot even allow herself to hear the name spoken aloud.
The phrase she uses to describe her situation is one I find genuinely chilling.
"Knowing that my mere existence as a living creature was an unforeseen danger in her way, I could not always conquer that terror of myself which had seized me when I first knew the secret."
'Terror of myself' — she has become afraid of her own being in the world.
That is not a Victorian melodrama convention — that is a precise psychological description of what it means to exist under a secret that threatens someone you love.

And it tells you something about the kind of novel this is — that the satirist who invented the Smallweed monkey-description and the Skimpole nectarines is the same writer who gave Esther that sentence.
The range is staggering — and it's all earned, none of it showy.
Dickens understood that if you make people laugh hard enough in one chapter, they'll trust you to break their hearts in the next.
That trust between writer and reader — it's exactly what we'll keep returning to as we move through this novel.
Coming up, we go deeper into the world Dickens built — its legal machinery, its class structures, and the individuals ground up inside them.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Jo's Plight and Social Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's most searing preoccupations: the machinery of injustice, and the human beings it grinds down.
At the centre of that grinding is Jo — the crossing-sweeper, the boy who knows almost nothing, and yet who Dickens makes the moral centre of the entire novel.
We have three brilliant guides with us today.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley — novelist and creative writing teacher — who reads Dickens as a craftsman reads a master: always asking how the effect is achieved.
Professor James Blackstone — legal and social historian — who knows what these institutions actually were and what they actually did to actual people.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, audiobook voice of legend — who hears Dickens the way Dickens intended: performed, embodied, alive.
Let's begin with Jo's testimony at the inquest — or rather, his attempted testimony.
The inquest scene is one of those passages where Dickens does something almost impossibly audacious.
He writes Jo's deposition not as reported speech but as a kind of staccato inventory of negatives.
Everything Jo doesn't have, doesn't know, has never been given.
Listen to the rhythm of it — it builds like a drumbeat.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words, then four words. And a universe of deprivation in ten syllables.
That is Dickens as a writer of absolute economy — when he wants to be.
And what strikes me is that Dickens doesn't let it be merely pathetic.
Jo is refused as a witness because the court decides he doesn't understand the oath.
And yet look at what Dickens actually gives him — a perfectly coherent moral framework.
The passage tells us Jo knows a broom is a broom and knows it's wicked to tell a lie.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
That's not the testimony of someone without moral understanding. That's ethics stripped to its essence.
The structural irony is vicious: the institution that claims to pursue truth dismisses the one witness who is determined to tell it.
And that irony is historically precise, not merely rhetorical.
In mid-Victorian England, witnesses at a coroner's inquest could be disqualified if they failed to demonstrate understanding of the Christian oath.
The practical effect was to exclude precisely those people — the uneducated, the destitute — most likely to be witnesses to deaths caused by poverty and neglect.
Dickens understood that the law's stated neutrality was in practice a class weapon.
Jo's exclusion is not a failure of the system — it is the system working exactly as designed.
Before we leave Jo's testimony entirely, can we spend a moment with Mrs. Piper?
Because she is the comic counterweight — and Dickens is too smart to keep the scene entirely in one register.
The narrator introduces her with magnificent condescension: she has, we're told, a good deal to say but not much to tell.
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
Chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation — that is a description of her syntax, and also of her mind.
And then she delivers this extraordinary legal concept: that the dead man — whom she insists on calling the plaintive — had reportedly sold himself.
The comedy is real, but it's not kind. These are the voices that shape the dead man's reputation in the absence of any other record.
That's exactly it — the grotesque and the tragic are doing the same work simultaneously.
Mrs. Piper's rambling testimony is funny, but it is also the noise that drowns out truth.
And then Dickens pivots — hard — to Jo's account of the dead man's actual kindness.
It's one of the most devastating juxtapositions in the novel. The community has nothing but rumour. Jo has this.
"Neither have I. Not one!" — and then the man gives Jo the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
Two outcasts recognising each other on a cold street. That is the novel's entire moral argument in a single gesture.
What that passage also shows is that the dead man — Nemo — has no social existence either.
Not one friend. No one who knows him. He is as legally and socially invisible as Jo is.
And yet he asks Jo whether he ever wished to die — and similar strange questions, as the text puts it.
"Whether he ever wished to die, and similar strange questions."
A man asking a street-sweeper whether he wishes to die is a man who has himself considered the question very seriously.
The law sees neither of them. Dickens makes certain we see both.
And then the narrator does something extraordinary in his own voice — he addresses Jo directly.
It's one of those moments where the machinery of the third-person narrator simply breaks — and the author steps through.
"Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness... thou art not quite in outer darkness."
The biblical register — thou, thy, outer darkness — is deliberate and devastating.
Dickens is not just defending Jo. He's canonising him.
And the proof of grace he offers is that muttered reason — the quote I find almost unbearable each time.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The misspelling is not mockery. It is love, rendered in the only language Jo has.
The novel doesn't confine its critique of power to the very poor, of course.
I want to bring in Tulkinghorn — because he represents a different and in some ways more insidious machinery.
Jo is destroyed by systemic neglect. Lady Dedlock is threatened by deliberate, personal, calculated power.
There is a scene where Lady Dedlock attempts to leave the room and Tulkinghorn stops her without moving a single muscle.
"Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
And then: 'And then I must speak out before every guest and servant, every man and woman, in it.'
The man doesn't raise his voice. He doesn't move. The threat is absolute because the information is absolute.
Knowledge, in this novel, is always power — and it is never exercised on behalf of the powerless.
Tulkinghorn is the novel's most technically frightening character, I think.
Because Dickens gives him almost no interiority. We never know what he wants beyond control itself.
And that stillness you described, James — 'without himself stirring hand or foot or raising his voice' — is a masterpiece of threatening prose.
The grammar enacts the threat. Every negated action — not stirring, not raising — creates the impression of a coiled, withheld violence.
Compare that to Jo, who has nothing to threaten with — only love, only gratitude, only those seven heartbreaking words.
And Dickens doesn't let that contrast stay merely implicit.
There's another moment — smaller, but it lodges in the mind. Mr. Jellyby's single piece of fatherly advice to Caddy.
This is a man who has been silenced for years by a household organised around a mission he was never consulted about.
And finally he speaks. And what he says is this.
"Never have a mission, my dear child."
Six words. The entire Jellyby catastrophe compressed into a plea.
And notice — that's the same number of words Jo needs. Both men speaking from the wreckage of what institutions have done to them.
That's a remarkable parallel to end on — two kinds of damage, two kinds of economy.
Jo with no language and all feeling. Mr. Jellyby with language, finally, and feeling that has nowhere else to go.
In the next segment we turn to the novel's other great system of cruelty — Chancery itself — and what it means that Bleak House begins and ends there.

segments.title: A Woman's Concealment: Lady Dedlock's Unravelling

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most gripping dramatic engines: Lady Dedlock's secret, and the slow, suffocating process by which it begins to unravel.
With me are Eleanor Hartley, who will be watching the architecture of how Dickens constructs concealment on the page.
James Blackstone, who brings the legal and social world that makes these secrets so dangerous.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who hears these scenes as a performer — and whose ear for Dickens's rhythms is, frankly, unrivalled.
Eleanor, let's begin with Tulkinghorn — this extraordinary figure who walks into Chesney Wold carrying, as Dickens puts it, something quite remarkable about his very person.
Yes — and Dickens gives us this figure before he gives us a word of dialogue, which is itself a structural choice worth pausing on.
He describes Tulkinghorn approaching at his usual methodical pace — never quickened, never slackened.
That repetition — never quickened, never slackened — is a tiny rhythmic closed door.
And then comes the sentence I find almost frightening in its compactness.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb, every crease — the man is not keeping secrets, he is made of them.
Dickens doesn't give us a character carrying a briefcase of documents — he gives us a body that is itself an archive.
That's a novelist thinking in images, not just in plot.
And the parenthetical — "if it be a mask" — is doing so much quiet work there.
Dickens slips in a doubt — is this expressionlessness performance, or is it simply what the man is?
And the answer he provides is brilliantly evasive.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients — he is his own client in that matter.
As a performer, I find that construction — he is his own client — almost vertiginous.
The man has lawyered himself against his own self-knowledge.
There's a very precise historical reality underneath that image, and it makes it darker still.
Victorian family solicitors of Tulkinghorn's type held an extraordinary position — they were not merely legal advisers but custodians of genealogical embarrassment.
They knew who had died in debt, who had married beneath themselves, who had produced children that could not be publicly acknowledged.
And crucially — they had no formal obligation of silence to anyone but their client.
Which means Lady Dedlock's danger is structural as much as personal.
And that danger becomes almost choreographic when they're actually in the same room together.
The passage describing their meetings at Chesney Wold — the way they perform not watching each other while absolutely watching each other — it reads almost like a duel in slow motion.
That passage opens with a detail that might seem incidental but is, I think, central.
Sir Leicester watches the fire — not his wife, not Tulkinghorn — the fire.
And Dickens tells us he does so with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.
He has been assimilated into the family portraiture — he is already a painting of himself, not a man capable of perceiving what is happening before him.
That is Dickens being quietly devastating about the English aristocracy — and quietly merciful to Lady Dedlock.
The structural comparison I keep returning to is the passage in chapter twelve where they meet repeatedly across several days.
Dickens describes Lady Dedlock as — and this phrase is so strange and precise —
"the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
Deity — but an exhausted one, presiding over worship she finds intolerable.
The irony is exquisitely calibrated: the social performance that protects her secret is also the thing slowly killing her.
The shrine and the prison are the same room.
And set against that, Tulkinghorn: "the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
She is everywhere and suffocated. He is nowhere and completely comfortable.
The power dynamic is entirely in that contrast.
And then Dickens delivers the great refrain of this whole section — the sentence that rolls back and forth like a tide.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
"What each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
For the time — those three words are doing the work of a whole act of theatre.
The anaphora of whether — whether... whether... what — it's not decoration, it's suspense made grammatical.
Each clause withholds its answer as it poses its question.
The reader is placed in exactly the same position as Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn — knowing that something is known, but not knowing how much.
And what Dickens reveals — gradually, through another character entirely — is the shape of the secret itself.
The chapters narrated by Esther Summerson give us the other side of this concealment — a child who was bred in secrecy, her very existence blotted out.
James, as a historian of social institutions — what does it mean, legally and socially, to have one's existence erased in this way?
It means, in practical terms, that you have no claim on anyone — no name that connects you to property, to lineage, to the law's protections.
And the letter that Jarndyce received — written with what he calls stern passion and power — describes exactly this annihilation.
The writer had bred the child in secrecy from her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence.
"She would be left entirely friendless, nameless, and unknown."
Friendless, nameless, unknown — three words, three different kinds of social death.
Without a name, you cannot inherit, you cannot sue, you cannot in any meaningful sense exist before the law.
What arrests me in Jarndyce's account is the phrase he uses for the letter itself: written with a stern passion and power that rendered it unlike all other letters I have ever read.
We never see that letter — Dickens never gives it to us directly.
What we get instead is a man so altered by reading it that he still reaches for superlatives nine years later.
And it was written to Jarndyce — this is Dickens being very deliberate — perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it.
"It was written to me, perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it."
Even that sentence keeps the mystery alive — it offers two reasons and commits to neither.
And the secret about the sender — her name was an assumed one — is delivered with the same evasive grammar.
Jarndyce reports: "That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt."
If — a conditional that does so much concealing work.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
For any human consideration — the resolution is absolute and total.
And that word steadfastness — it's not cold, it's desperate.
The passage that gives me most pause — in the worst way — is the one describing why the child had been made to suffer.
Jarndyce describes it as a distorted religion — and this is one of the more searing indictments in the whole novel.
"The distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent."
The child must expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent.
Dickens uses the word distorted, and it's precise — this isn't religion, it's guilt that has borrowed religion's vocabulary to torture a child.
The mother's shame has been transferred onto the daughter as a theological debt she was born owing.
Jarndyce's response to all of this — and it's the most unguarded he ever is — is simply: I felt concerned for the little creature in her darkened life.
Little creature — not child, not orphan — creature.
It's the word you use when something is so diminished, so reduced, that it barely has human standing yet.
And then: in her darkened life.
Not difficult life, not unfortunate life — darkened.
Light deliberately withheld.
Light deliberately withheld — and yet Esther Summerson becomes one of the warmest presences in the novel.

What we've traced today is the extraordinary geometry of Lady Dedlock's secret — how it shapes Tulkinghorn, how it shaped the woman herself into a deity of performance, and how it shaped the child she was never permitted to acknowledge.
Eleanor, James, Oliver — thank you.
We'll be back with more from Bleak House — a novel that hides its most important truths in the same place it always does: in plain sight.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We're deep into the novel now, and one of its most quietly devastating threads is already in motion: the fate of Richard Carstone.
Richard is young, charming, well-liked — and constitutionally incapable of applying himself to anything.
Today we're looking at Chapter Thirteen and Seventeen — passages where Dickens lays the groundwork for one of literature's most painful character arcs.
Eleanor Hartley is here to trace the novel's architectural choices — the way Dickens builds doom into what looks like a scene of tenderness.
James Blackstone will bring us the institutional and moral context — what it actually meant to drift through professions in Victorian England.
And Oliver Trevelyan will do what he does best — listen to the prose itself, and hear what it's really saying beneath the surface warmth.
What strikes me first about these Chapter Thirteen passages is how cunningly Dickens uses a scene of genuine tenderness to install a structural alarm.
Esther is sitting between Ada and Richard, and she tells us — almost apologetically — that she never stopped their romantic effusions.
She says, and this is the setup for everything,

"it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Three nouns — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — and Richard will fail every single one of them.
Dickens plants the verdict before the trial has even begun.
And the moment you hear those three words aloud, you feel the irony land — because Richard, bless him, has just promised to work his fingers to the bone.
Which is exactly the kind of magnificent, theatrical promise that a young man makes when he has absolutely no intention of doing anything of the sort.
Then Mr. Jarndyce steps in, and this is where Dickens gives us the true moral axis of the scene.
Jarndyce says — and I could perform this speech every night of the week —
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that image is pure Dickens: completely unexpected, perfectly precise.
The man who prays for his cart to be freed from the mud without putting his shoulder to the wheel.
That is Richard, exactly — and Jarndyce knows it.
What Jarndyce is articulating is a very specific Victorian ethic — the idea that Providence and self-reliance are not in tension but are, in fact, identical.
To rely on Providence without effort is not piety; it is laziness dressed in religious language.
And Jarndyce puts it with a directness that is almost alarming, given how gently he has handled the children up to this point.

He tells Richard: "If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
That is an ultimatum — and a remarkably clear-eyed one from a guardian who is usually all weather-vanes and east winds.
The tragedy, of course, is that Richard hears it and feels it — and then forgets it almost immediately.
And then Dickens does something formally extraordinary, which James's point sets up beautifully.
After all the advice, all the warmth, all the good counsel — Esther watches Ada and Richard walk away through the sunlit rooms.
And the prose shifts register entirely. Listen to this:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Three sentences — and Dickens has written a complete tragedy in miniature.
The pathetic fallacy here isn't decoration — it's verdict.
That passage stops me every time I read it aloud.
"Passed away into the shadow and were gone" — that's a funeral phrase, dropped into the middle of what should be a hopeful scene.
Dickens is telling us, in the quietest possible voice, that what we have just witnessed is a kind of ending.
And then Chapter Seventeen arrives, and Mrs. Badger — magnificently, mercilessly — makes it all explicit.
She tells Esther, with that particular brand of genteel surgical precision, that Richard simply lacks the vocation.

And she puts Woodcourt beside him as the contrast: "Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
There's Woodcourt — the man Esther loves, not incidentally — defined entirely by the qualities Richard cannot summon.
Dickens is doing several things at once, and doing all of them perfectly.
Mrs. Badger's diagnosis is worth pausing on, because historically it maps onto something very real about how professions worked in this period.
Medicine, law, the church, the military — these were not simply careers. They were social identities, each with their own culture of belonging.
A young man of Richard's class who drifted through them was not merely wasting time — he was announcing, publicly, that he had no fixed self.
And Jarndyce had already spotted this, back in the scene Eleanor described — though he framed it as tenderness rather than warning.
He told Richard and Ada: "don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it" — if they change, if their love fades.
That phrase — nothing monstrous or uncommon — is Jarndyce keeping the door open, because he has already sensed what is coming.
He is the wisest man in this novel, and wisdom here looks a great deal like grief held in reserve.
That is beautifully put — and it loops back to the craft question for me.
Dickens doesn't make Jarndyce a pessimist. He makes him a realist who chooses, generously, to act as if optimism might still win.
The structure of these scenes — tenderness, warning, foreboding image — follows a tragic arc with the precision of music.
Introduction of theme, development, recapitulation in shadow.
And we're only in Chapter Thirteen. Richard has barely started falling.
The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over — and as Oliver said, Dickens has already written the ending into the beginning.
That is what we mean when we talk about architecture in the novel — and why these early chapters reward such close attention.
Coming up: we turn to the fog — literal and legal — and what it means that this novel opens not with a character, but with a climate.

segments.title: Dickens's Fractured Narrative: Form and Meaning

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great, sprawling masterpiece apart sentence by sentence to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at something that sits right at the heart of the novel: how Dickens constructs meaning through form — through the very shape and voice of his storytelling.
With me today are three remarkable readers of this book, each bringing a completely different lens.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how great fiction is actually built — the architecture beneath the surface.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real world of Victorian institutions alive — the courts, the poverty, the system — in ways that make the novel newly urgent.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and the voice of more classic audiobooks than I can count — someone who hears Dickens with his whole body, as performance.
Today's segment asks: what does Dickens's fractured, dual-narrator structure actually do — what meanings does it make possible that no other arrangement could?
Eleanor, you've been thinking hard about the narration — shall we start with you?
Yes — and I want to start not with the famous double narration itself, but with what Esther's voice is allowed to see that the omniscient narrator simply cannot.
There's a passage early on where Esther watches two women — coarse, shabby, beaten, as she puts it — comforting each other.
And out of that observation, Dickens delivers one of the most quietly devastating lines in the entire novel.
Esther says:
"I think the best side of such people is almost hidden from us. What the poor are to the poor is little known, excepting to themselves and God."
That sentence does something technically extraordinary: it implicates Esther in the blindness she's naming.
She is one of "us" — the observer, however compassionate — and she knows it.
No omniscient narrator could carry that particular moral weight with such precision.
And that observation has a very specific historical bite, of course.
The charitable and reforming classes of the 1850s were endlessly writing reports about the poor — cataloguing their conditions, their moral failings, their domestic arrangements.
What Esther names here — that the inner life of poor communities is simply not legible to outsiders — is a genuine epistemological problem that those reports never grasped.
Dickens understood it.
What strikes me performing that line is how much Dickens has packed into the word "excepting."
"Excepting to themselves and God" — that small exception contains an entire theology of suffering.
God is not a comfort here so much as a witness — the only witness.
And then, just a few chapters later, those same women — Jenny and Liz — are given a moment that earns that observation completely.
Jenny speaks about her dead child and her living friend's child, and the speech she's given is — I find it almost unbearable to read.

"It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear, and it's my dead child that makes her love it so dear too... we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!"
"Us two mothers does" — that grammatical irregularity is not a mistake. It is the voice.
Yes — and notice what Dickens has done structurally: he sets up the thesis in Esther's narration, then proves it through direct speech in the omniscient chapters.
The two narrative streams aren't just alternating — they're in dialogue.
They answer each other.
And the emotional intelligence of that speech — Jenny articulating a grief she admits she barely has words for — that is what Esther predicted we couldn't see from the outside.
Now we see it. Dickens makes us see it.
That interplay between the two narrative streams is something I want to stay with — but I'd like to bring in Richard Carstone, because his story offers a completely different kind of fracture.
Eleanor, you've been looking at the passage where Richard tries to explain himself to Esther — can you take us into it?
Richard's speech here is one of the great moments of self-diagnosis in all of Victorian fiction.
He constructs a metaphor — the unfinished house — that is both completely lucid and completely tragic.
He says to Esther:
"If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn't settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything."
And then he applies it directly to himself:
"I was born into this unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it has gone on unsettling me ever since."
The word "unsettling" does triple duty there — legal uncertainty, psychological instability, moral drift.
Dickens has hidden an entire character study inside one repeated verb.
The metaphor is precise in a way Richard himself probably doesn't fully intend.
Chancery suits in this period could genuinely last generations — not metaphorically, but literally.
Richard has been designated an interested party in Jarndyce and Jarndyce since birth — his entire legal identity is wrapped up in proceedings he cannot control and cannot escape.
So when he describes himself as born into an unfinished contention, that is not poetic license.
That is the literal legal fact of his existence.
What breaks me in that speech is the end of it.
He says he is sometimes conscious that he is "but a worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada."
He knows. He sees himself with terrible clarity in that moment.
And it doesn't save him.
That is where Dickens is utterly merciless — self-knowledge in Bleak House is never redemptive.
Self-knowledge without redemption — that's a very dark note.
But the novel does offer something else — at least in Esther's world.
There's that extraordinary moment when Ada sees Esther's changed face for the first time, after her illness.
Eleanor — what is happening there, in terms of how Esther narrates it?
This is one of the most technically daring moments in Esther's entire narrative, and it goes by in three lines.
Ada runs in, sees Esther — her face after the smallpox — and Esther describes what she reads there:
"The old dear look, all love, all fondness, all affection. Nothing else in it — no, nothing, nothing!"
That triple "nothing" is not emphasis — it's refutation.
Esther has been dreading disgust, or pity disguised as love — and she is refusing to find it.
The repetition is the action of a mind checking, double-checking, reassuring itself.
Dickens renders interiority not through reported thought but through the rhythm of the sentence itself.
"Ah, my angel girl!" — that exclamation just before it.
When you read this aloud, that break changes everything.
It's an almost helpless outburst from Esther — and then she immediately controls herself and observes.
That compression — feeling and analysis in the same breath — is the hallmark of her narration throughout the novel.
And worth noting: this is a woman who has been told her entire life that she is a burden, a shame, someone who should be grateful for small mercies.
For Esther to read Ada's face so carefully, to insist so hard on what is not there — pity, revulsion, withdrawal — that is not mere sentiment.
That is a woman who has learned to expect the worst from the world and is being, in this one moment, surprised by love.
Surprised by love — in a novel that is otherwise so unsparing about institutions, about the damage systems do to people.
We've seen today how the dual narration isn't a structural quirk — it's the argument of the book.
The form is the meaning: two voices, two ways of knowing, and between them the whole of the novel's moral world.
We'll be back after the break to look at Chancery itself — the great machine at the centre of the novel and what Dickens does with it.

segments.title: Dark Comedy and Bleak Satire: The Wit Within the Mire

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take our time with one of the great novels in the English language.
Today's segment takes us into territory that makes this novel so unsettling and so brilliant — the way Dickens deploys comedy right next to devastation.
With me are three extraordinary guides to this world.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for fictional craft is, frankly, formidable.
Prof. James Blackstone brings legal and social history — he'll tell us what these institutions actually were, and why that matters.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more great novels aloud than perhaps anyone living — hears this text as performance first.
We're looking today at two very different kinds of Dickensian darkness — the savage comedy of political satire, and the tender grief of a boy no one cares about.
Oliver, I want to start with you — because the Boodle and Noodle passage is, on its face, hilarious. What are we actually laughing at?
What we're laughing at — and I want to be precise about this — is the names.
Boodle, Coodle, Doodle, Foodle — Dickens is doing something deceptively simple: he's built an entire governing class out of a single nursery rhyme syllable.
And the brilliance is that the joke doesn't exhaust itself — it accumulates.
By the time we reach Poodle and Quoodle, we've understood something devastating: these men are interchangeable, and they know it, and they don't care.
Then Dickens lands the punchline with absolute precision.
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces — as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock — because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The country. Shipwrecked. Because of Noodle.
And the institutional accuracy underneath that comedy is what makes it sting rather than merely tickle.
This is precisely how Cabinet formation worked in mid-Victorian Britain — a closed circulation of aristocratic and landed interest.
Dickens assigns every major office of state — the Home Department, the Exchequer, the Foreign Office — and the whole exercise is about accommodating the men, not governing the country.
Lord Boodle tells Sir Leicester this with what Dickens calls 'much gravity, after dinner' — and those four words do the real satirical work.
The solemnity, the digestion, the port — all of it is undisturbed by the absurdity of what's being said.
What strikes me structurally is that this passage has no dramatic tension of its own — and that's entirely deliberate.
Dickens builds it as a single, extended sentence that just keeps adding names — Hoodle, Joodle, Koodle — and the form mirrors the content perfectly.
The sentence has nowhere to go because these men have nowhere to go — they can only shuffle offices among themselves.
And crucially, the satire is delivered through free indirect discourse — we're inside Lord Boodle's earnest, unironic perspective.
He genuinely believes the country will be shipwrecked. That sincerity is the engine of the comedy.
Eleanor's absolutely right — and as a performer, that free indirect discourse is the gift.
You play it straight. Absolutely straight. With all the earnestness of a man who has dined very well.
And yet — and this is the thing about Bleak House — the comedy never exists in isolation.
In the very same chapter we get Jo — the crossing-sweeper — grieving at the gate of a pauper's cemetery.
James, what's the social reality that sits behind Jo's grief?
Jo is, historically speaking, one of tens of thousands — children who lived entirely outside any institutional framework of care.
No parish, no school, no family of record. A street child who sweeps crossings for pennies flung from a carriage.
And the man he's mourning — Nemo — is a pauper buried in one of the notorious urban burial grounds that Victorian reformers spent decades trying to close down.
Overcrowded, insanitary, without markers or records. People shovelled in.
That Jo comes back to sweep the step clean is not incidental sentiment — it is the only form of rite this dead man will receive.
And look at what Dickens does with the pronoun. This is the thing that stopped me cold when I first read it closely.
He doesn't write 'Jo sweeps the step.' He writes —
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
'It.' A child reduced to a neuter pronoun. Society has already decided Jo is not quite a person.
And yet the act described — softly sweeping, making clean — is one of the most human and loving gestures in the novel.
Dickens puts those two things in absolute collision in a single sentence.
When you read that passage aloud — and I have, more than once — the 'it' lands like a wound.
But what finishes me — every time — is what Jo says earlier, about the dead man.
It's just a boy wiping his eyes on a wretched sleeve. And then —
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The misspelling — 'wos,' 'wery' — is doing double work there.
It renders the dialect exactly, which makes it true — and it makes us hear a child who has had almost nothing, describing the one person who was kind to him.
And then Dickens adds 'he wos!' again, at the end. The repetition. That's not grammar — that's a broken heart.
That dialect is a deliberate provocation too, historically speaking.
Dickens is forcing his middle-class readership to hear a voice they would have walked past every day without listening to.
Jo cannot read, cannot write, cannot 'give no name to nothing in any ways whatsoever,' as Dickens has him say elsewhere.
But he can grieve. He can be grateful. He comes back in the night, as the text puts it —
"With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate. It holds the gate with its hands and looks in between the bars."
That image — the hands on the iron bars — is one of the great images of exclusion in Victorian fiction.
On the other side: a dead man. On this side: the one person in London who mourns him.
And that image sits in the same novel as Boodle, Doodle, and Noodle arguing about Cabinet posts.
I think that's the formal argument of Bleak House, stated in structure rather than speech.
The country is, as Lord Boodle would say, shipwrecked — because while the Noodles and Poodles carve up the offices of state, there is a child in the dark holding on to a cemetery gate.
That structural argument — comedy and tragedy not alternating but simultaneous — is what we'll keep returning to throughout this episode.
The wit and the grief arrive together in Bleak House, and neither lets the other off the hook.
After the break, we'll turn to the novel's two narrators — and the very different worlds they're permitted to see.

segments.title: Closing: Fog Descends—The Weight of Systems

utterances.text: We've spent this episode inside the fog—Chancery's fog, Chesney Wold's fog, the fog that Dickens makes us feel in our bones.
Before we close, I want to bring James back to something that has been threading through everything we've discussed today—the question of whether any of it can change.
James, you've been sitting with some passages that go right to the heart of that question.
Yes—and what strikes me most, returning to these passages now, is how Dickens anatomises the machinery of self-preservation.
There is a moment in chapter thirty-nine that I find almost unbearably precise about how institutional reform is defeated.
Mr. Kenge is defending the legal system to a client who is being destroyed by it.
And the argument he deploys is not that the system is just—he essentially concedes it is not—but that its practitioners must be preserved.
He says—and this is the crux—
"Now you cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose an order of men like Mr. Vholes."
The social system cannot afford it.
Vholes's respectability is not incidental — it is the actual instrument of obstruction.
What kills me about that passage is the mock parliamentary inquiry that follows.
Dickens numbers the question—five hundred and seventeen thousand, eight hundred and sixty-nine.
That grotesque number is doing so much work — it's the weight of bureaucracy rendered as comedy.
And then the whole inquiry collapses on a single sentence.
"Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man."
—which, Dickens notes, proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
That parenthetical aside is one of the sharpest things in the novel.
Ten years.
One word — respectable — and the whole machinery of reform grinds to a halt for a decade.
And then Vholes himself — in chapter sixty — carries this same performance of professional duty to Esther.
He tells her that he noted the very words he used to her in his diary — producible at any time, he says.
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out.
But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
Every syllable is armour.
He is honest — technically, scrupulously honest — and Richard Carstone is being consumed alive.
But Dickens does something that I think is often underrated — he doesn't just indict the system.
He places against all of this — the paralysis of law, the armour of respectability — a moment of absolute human vulnerability.
Mrs. Rouncewell, in chapter fifty-five, pleading with Lady Dedlock for her son's life.
"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know;
if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
That repetition — pray, oh, pray — is not rhetoric.
It is the sound of someone who has exhausted every other form of address and is simply begging.
And what Dickens does with Sir Leicester in chapter fifty-eight is the other side of that coin.
Leicester Dedlock, of all people — the most encrusted figure in the novel's establishment — earns a moment of genuine moral radiance.
The narrator says his fidelity, his gallant shielding of Lady Dedlock, his conquest of his own pride for her sake, are simply honourable.
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
Children of the dust.
That phrase dismantles the entire class hierarchy of the novel in five words.
Dickens grants Leicester his dignity not by dissolving the social world, but by finding the human beneath it.
That's what I find myself thinking about at the end of Bleak House — not the systems, but the people who survive inside them.
Mrs. Rouncewell on her knees.
Sir Leicester, stricken but unbroken.
Vholes, noting everything in his diary, charging nothing — and ruining Richard with perfect professional courtesy.
Dickens holds all of this simultaneously — the comic grotesque and the genuinely tragic — and never flinches.
That's what makes Bleak House feel less like a novel than like — life.
Less like a novel than like life.
I think that's the most honest summary of this book I've ever heard.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — three readers who have made the fog feel, if anything, richer for navigating it together.
Bleak House Unpacked will return.
Until then — keep reading.

bottle of light wine. Mr. Skimpole himself reclined upon the sofa in

c36:p32.text:
I raised my mother up, praying and beseeching her not to stoop before
me in such affliction and humiliation. I did so in broken, incoherent
words, for besides the trouble I was in, it frightened me to see her
at MY feet. I told her—or I tried to tell her—that if it were for
me, her child, under any circumstances to take upon me to forgive
her, I did it, and had done it, many, many years. I told her that my
heart overflowed with love for her, that it was natural love which
nothing in the past had changed or could change. That it was not for
me, then resting for the first time on my mother’s bosom, to take her
to account for having given me life, but that my duty was to bless
her and receive her, though the whole world turned from her, and that
I only asked her leave to do it. I held my mother in my embrace, and
she held me in hers, and among the still woods in the silence of the
summer day there seemed to be nothing but our two troubled minds that
was not at peace.
c36:p32.summary: Esther raises her mother from her knees, speaking in broken, emotional words about forgiving her long ago and expressing that her deepest duty is to bless and receive her unconditionally.
c36:p32.best_quote: my duty was to bless her and receive her, though the whole world turned from her, and that I only asked her leave to do it.

c43:p0.text:
It matters little now how much I thought of my living mother who had
told me evermore to consider her dead. I could not venture to
approach her or to communicate with her in writing, for my sense of
the peril in which her life was passed was only to be equalled by my
fears of increasing it. Knowing that my mere existence as a living
creature was an unforeseen danger in her way, I could not always
conquer that terror of myself which had seized me when I first knew
the secret. At no time did I dare to utter her name. I felt as if I
did not even dare to hear it. If the conversation anywhere, when I
was present, took that direction, as it sometimes naturally did, I
tried not to hear: I mentally counted, repeated something that I
knew, or went out of the room. I am conscious now that I often did
these things when there can have been no danger of her being spoken
of, but I did them in the dread I had of hearing anything that might
lead to her betrayal, and to her betrayal through me.
c43:p0.summary: Esther describes the anguish of living in proximity to her mother while maintaining absolute distance, unable even to speak her name or hear it mentioned without psychological distress.
c43:p0.best_quote: Knowing that my mere existence as a living creature was an unforeseen danger in her way, I could not always conquer that terror of myself which had seized me when I first knew the secret.

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

c12:p67.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. c12:p114.text:
During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady
Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their
customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as
was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject. Sir
Leicester has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the
Dedlock on the staircase. The story being told, he renews his stately
protest, saying that as it is quite clear that no association in my
Lady’s mind can possibly be traceable to this poor wretch (unless he
was a begging-letter writer), he trusts to hear no more about a
subject so far removed from my Lady’s station.
c12:p114.summary: Throughout the exchange, Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn watch each other intently while maintaining composure; Sir Leicester watches the fire. The narrative reveals their mutual suspicion and hidden knowledge.
c12:p114.best_quote: During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

c12:p116.text:
Mr. Tulkinghorn does so with deference and holds it open while she
passes out. She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner
and insolent grace. They meet again at dinner—again, next

Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble

reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the

seclusion, written with a stern passion and power that rendered it
unlike all other letters I have ever read. It was written to me (as

idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to
justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years
old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your
remembrance. It told me that the writer had bred her in secrecy from
her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence, and that if

consider if I would, in that case, finish what the writer had begun.”

There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through
the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the
years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed
away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that
had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”

c8:p105.text:

and beaten, so united; to see what they could be to one another; to

c23:p41.text:
“You are kinder to me than I often am to myself,” he returned. “My
dear Esther, I am a very unfortunate dog not to be more settled, but
how CAN I be more settled? If you lived in an unfinished house, you
couldn’t settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything
you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to
anything; and yet that’s my unhappy case. I was born into this
unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it began
to unsettle me before I quite knew the difference between a suit at
law and a suit of clothes; and it has gone on unsettling me ever
since; and here I am now, conscious sometimes that I am but a
worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada.”

c36:p79.text:
She ran in, and was running out again when she saw me. Ah, my angel

c12:p56.text:
Then there is my Lord Boodle, of considerable reputation with his
party, who has known what office is and who tells Sir Leicester
Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see
to what the present age is tending. A debate is not what a debate
used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a
Cabinet is not what it formerly was. He perceives with astonishment
that supposing the present government to be overthrown, the limited
choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
assumed to be the case in consequence of the breach arising out of
that affair with Hoodle. Then, giving the Home Department and the
leadership of the House of Commons to Joodle, the Exchequer to
Koodle, the Colonies to Loodle, and the Foreign Office to Moodle,
what are you to do with Noodle? You can’t offer him the Presidency of
the Council; that is reserved for Poodle. You can’t put him in the
Woods and Forests; that is hardly good enough for Quoodle. What
follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces
(as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock)
because you can’t provide for Noodle!

But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.

c60:p94.text:
“Pardon me,” returned Mr. Vholes, going on in exactly the same inward
and dispassionate manner. “Mr. C. takes certain interests under
certain wills disputed in the suit. It is a term we use. In reference
to Mr. C,’s pursuit of his interests, I mentioned to you, Miss
Summerson, the first time I had the pleasure of seeing you, in my
desire that everything should be openly carried on—I used those
words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down
the principle of watching his own interests, and that when a client
of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I
regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage. Am I here, sir?
Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of
some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to
thank you very much, sir!”

c55:p71.text:
“Hush! Hush!” The housekeeper looks round and answers in a frightened
whisper, “My Lady, I have not breathed a word of it, I don’t believe
what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain
that it is not true. But my son is in danger, and you must have a
heart to pity me. If you know of anything that is not known to
others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think
of me, and conquer that reason, and let it be known! This is the most
I consider possible. I know you are not a hard lady, but you go your
own way always without help, and you are not familiar with your
friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,
but I feel so much that I have come here to make so bold as to beg
and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or
justice at this fearful time!”
c55:p71.summary: Mrs. Rouncewell delivers a long, passionate plea to Lady Dedlock, urging her to conquer her pride and help clear her innocent son if she knows any truth or clue.

c58:p70.text:
His formal array of words might have at any other time, as it has
often had, something ludicrous in it, but at this time it is serious
and affecting. His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant
shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own
pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true. Nothing
less worthy can be seen through the lustre of such qualities in the
commonest mechanic, nothing less worthy can be seen in the best-born
gentleman. In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both
children of the dust shine equally.
c58:p70.summary: The narrator reflects that Sir Leicester's earnestness, fidelity, and generous conquering of his own pride for Lady Dedlock's sake transcend class and honor all humanity.
